lesson_title: The Antelope That Runs a Fever on Purpose
hook_text: A gemsbok lets its body heat past 45 degrees and does not die. That trick is the whole idea of adaptation, and it has a dark ending.
clip_script: Kalahari sand, over 60 degrees, no water for months. The gemsbok is built for it. Pale coat to bounce off the sun: a part, a structural adaptation. It lets its body temperature climb past 45 degrees instead of sweating away water, and cools the blood going to its brain through a network in its nose: a process, a functional adaptation. It feeds at night when plants are juiciest and digs up water-filled melons: a habit, a behavioural adaptation. Part, process, habit. Every adaptation is an inherited feature that fits a creature to its home, and only that home; a polar bear's coat would kill it here. Now the dark ending. When the home changes faster than the creature can, when the grass becomes a sheep farm and the hunter has a rifle, the species dies out. The quagga, a Karoo zebra with stripes only on its neck, was shot out by the 1870s. The last one died in a zoo in 1883. Extinct means gone everywhere, for ever.
visual_style: A gemsbok outline with three callouts labelled part, process, habit; then a sepia photograph frame of a quagga with the date 1883 stamped across it.
pacing: Hot, quick opening, three crisp labels, a slow turn to the quagga, one hard final line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort any adaptation into part, process or habit.
